evidence: Cic. Att. 8.4.2: numquam reō cuiquam … tam praecīsē negāvī quam hic mihi
Caes. B.G. 5.6 (Lewis & Short): postquam id obstinātē sibi negārī videt
terms.comment: The thing refused in the accusative, the person in the dative: negāre alicui aliquid. Its first sense is to deny that something is so (see deny).

evidence: Plaut. Trin. 1170–1171: sī tibi dēnegem quod mē ōrās
Caes. B.G. 1.42 (Lewis & Short): cum id quod anteā petentī dēnegāsset, ultrō pollicērētur
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: rarely “say it is not so”, far more often to refuse a request.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, an infinitive, or nē, quīn, quōminus
evidence: Caes. B.G. 7.2 (Lewis & Short): nūllum perīculum commūnis salūtis causā
terms.comment: To decline something offered or a task, or object to it, where negō refuses something asked of one.

phrases.latin: metuō, sī tibi dēnegem quod mē ōrās, nē tē leviōrem ergā mē putēs
phrases.english: I’m afraid that if I refuse what you ask me, you’ll think I value you less

phrases.latin: numquam reō cuiquam tam humilī, tam sordidō, tam nocentī, tam aliēnō tam praecīsē negāvī quam hic mihi
phrases.english: I never refused any defendant, however low, mean, guilty or remote from me, as flatly as he refused me

sources: Lewis & Short: nego · Lewis & Short: denego · Lewis & Short: recuso
